title: Enabling bainitic transformation acceleration and mechanical properties improvement in ultrafine bainitic steel
abstract: A novel approach involving the fast heating of cold-rolled pearlite followed by low-temperature isothermal transformation (FBT) was devised to address the technical challenges of long processing times and strength-ductility trade-off in ultrafine bainitic steels. Compared to conventional treatment (CBT), the FBT process yielded chemically heterogeneous bainite, along with refined austenite grain size, decreased retained austenite fraction and reduced dimension of blocky retained austenite. This heterogeneity was primarily manifested in the form of coarse filmy retained austenite with significant compositional fluctuations. The FBT process accelerated the bainitic transformation kinetics, which is attributed to the increased nucleation sites from prior austenite grain refinement and preferential nucleation at Mn-/Cr-depleted regions within the chemically heterogeneous austenite. Consequently, the FBT sample exhibited superior tensile properties, which are rationalized by the distinct retained austenite transformation behaviors. Interrupted tensile tests revealed that the CBT sample underwent a rapid transformation of unstable blocky retained austenite at low strains, while the FBT sample exhibited a progressive strain-induced transformation of its coarse filmy retained austenite, enabling a sustained transformation-induced plasticity effect. A key commonality was the exceptional stability of the fine filmy retained austenite in both samples, which persisted even after tensile fracture.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The mechanical properties of ultrafine bainitic steel depend mainly on the characteristics of bainitic ferrite (BF) and retained austenite (RA) [ 1–4 ]. The morphology and distribution of these phases are primarily determined by the selected isothermal transformation parameters, specifically temperature and time. Higher isothermal temperatures accelerate bainitic transformation but at the expense of coarsening the bainitic plates and degrading the strength [ 5 , 6 ]. Conversely, lower transformation temperatures refine the microstructure yet markedly retard the transformation kinetics and often compromise ductility [ 6–8 ]. This highlights a critical trade-off between achieving fast processing and obtaining optimal mechanical properties. Thus, developing heat treatment processes that offer the possibility to simultaneously accelerate phase transformation and achieve superior performance has emerged as a critical research objective.

It has been established that macroscopic elemental segregation exerts a detrimental effect on the bainitic transformation. This deleterious effect stems from the low diffusivity of austenite-stabilizing elements (e.g., Mn, Cr and Ni) and the associated solute drag effect, which mainly impedes the migration of the bainitic transformation interface and reduces the driving force for austenite to ferrite transformation, leading to pronounced phase transformation retardation [ 9–11 ]. However, Lan et al. [ 12 ] demonstrated that the intragranular chemical heterogeneity, established by Mn partitioning during intercritical annealing, facilitated bainitic transformation. Furthermore, the subsequent progressive transformation of the resulting metastable RA of varying stability during deformation effectively improved ductility and toughness. Similarly, Xu et al. [ 13 ] produced spheroidized cementite precursor enriched with Mn via salt bath annealing. These cementite particles provided favorable sites for bainite nucleation, effectively promoting the phase transformation. By employing intercritical annealing to create Mn-depleted ferrite, researchers leveraged this microstructural inheritance to form Mn-heterogeneous austenite [ 14 ]. The preferential bainitic formation in these Mn-depleted zones increased the density of spontaneous nucleation sites. Consequently, microscopic chemical heterogeneity presents a promising strategy for controlling bainitic transformation and mechanical properties. Nevertheless, all the aforementioned methods require prolonged pre-treatment times, extending the overall processing cycle.

Recent advances demonstrate that fast heating (defined as a heating rate ≥100  o C/s) may promote non-equilibrium interactions of elemental diffusion and phase transformations, facilitating the formation of multi-scale heterogeneous microstructures that concurrently enhance strength and toughness [ 15–20 ]. Fast heating has emerged as a promising route for improving the plastic deformability of advanced high-strength steels (e.g., medium-Mn, Q&P and nanobainitic steels). A key advantage of this approach is its ability to preserve the chemical heterogeneity of the initial microstructure, which is critical for tailoring the austenite stability. To simultaneously enhance strength and ductility, some researchers [ 15 , 16 ] leveraged the kinetic mismatch inherent in fast heating by starting from a pre-existing multiphase (cementite/austenite/ferrite) microstructure. This process created a heterogeneous Mn distribution in austenite, thereby stabilizing the Mn-enriched RA and leading to superior mechanical properties in medium-Mn steels. Similarly, Xiong et al. [ 17–19 ] employed a fast heating-isothermal quenching process based on lamellar pearlite to tailor the Mn heterogeneity in austenite. The resulting transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect was effectively leveraged to enhance the formability of heterogeneous Q&P steel. Chemical heterogeneity introduced via the fast heating of pearlitic precursors and subsequent austempering has also been exploited by researchers to engineer the microstructure of high-carbon bainitic steels [ 20–22 ]. This heterogeneity, particularly in Mn, accelerates the bainitic transformation kinetics and ultimately enhances the strength-ductility synergy. However, a systematic investigation into the effect of chemical heterogeneity resulting from fast heating on bainitic transformation kinetics and mechanical properties of medium-carbon low-alloy ultrafine bainitic steel remains lacking.

To address the technical challenges posed by time-consuming nature and strength-ductility trade-off in ultrafine bainitic steels, a processing route combining fast heating with low temperature isothermal transformation was proposed. Through multi-scale microstructure characterization and mechanical properties analysis, the evolution mechanism of metastable RA with multi-scale and chemical heterogeneity during tensile deformation was systematically investigated. This work aims to develop a novel medium-carbon, low-alloy ultrafine bainitic steel that exhibits a superior combination of strength and ductility coupled with a short process cycle.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
The material investigated in this study was a medium-carbon low-alloy steel with the following nominal chemical composition (in wt.%): 0.34C-2.0Si-1.8Mn-2.1Cr-0.8Ni. It was fabricated through vacuum induction melting, forging, homogenization and hot rolling. Phase transformation temperatures were measured on cylindrical samples (Φ 4 mm × 10 mm) taken from the hot-rolled plate using a DIL 805A dilatometer. The Ac 1 , Ac 3  and Ms temperatures were determined to be approximately 750, 860 and 290 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/s and a cooling rate of 20 °C/s, respectively. However, under a high heating rate of 100 °C/s, the Ac 1  and Ac 3  temperatures increased to 770 and 880 °C, respectively. This observation aligns with the documented phenomenon that fast heating raises transformation temperatures [ 23 ]. Accordingly, an austenitizing temperature of Ac 3  + 50 °C (930 °C) was employed in the subsequent experiments to guarantee complete austenitization.  Fig. 1 
                       shows the two different heat treatment schedules employed. As illustrated in  Fig. 1 (a), hot-rolled samples were austenitized at 930 °C for 15 min, followed by quenching into a high-temperature salt bath at 650 °C and isothermal holding for 4 h. The resulting material was cold-rolled with a 70 % thickness reduction, obtaining an initial microstructure of cold-rolled pearlite. Subsequently, the cold-rolled samples were rapidly heated to 930 °C at a rate of approximately 100  o C/s and held for 3 s to achieve austenitization, followed by immediate transfer to a 320 °C salt bath for 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 60 and 90 min prior to air cooling (abbreviated as FBT-t, where t denotes the isothermal time). For comparison, the conventional bainitic treatment (CBT-t) was also conducted. This process involved austenitization in a muffle furnace at a slow heating rate of approximately 10 °C/s for a prolonged duration of 15 min, followed by the same isothermal treatment as detailed in  Fig. 1 (b).

Microstructure observations were conducted using field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM), transmission electron microscope (TEM) and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). SEM samples were prepared by grinding, mechanical polishing and chemically etching with a 4 % nitric acid alcohol solution. Thin foils for TEM were prepared by mechanical grinding to 50 μm, punching into 3 mm discs and twin-jet electropolishing to perforation using a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid in ethanol at −30 °C and 25 V. EBSD was performed at an operating voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 0.05 μm. Phase analysis was conducted using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation. The scanning angles (2θ) ranged from 47° to 93°. Samples for EBSD and XRD analysis were prepared by electropolishing at 20 V for 15 s using a solution of 20 % perchloric acid in alcohol. The changes in RA volume fraction as a function of tensile strain were quantified using XRD, by calculating the diffraction peaks for (200)α, (211)α, (200)γ, (220)γ and (311)γ [ 24 ]. Tensile properties were determined using a universal testing machine at a strain rate of 6.667 × 10 −4  s −1  on specimens with parallel dimensions of 25 × 6 × 2 mm 3 . The strain was measured using a high-resolution extensometer with a gauge length of 25 mm, providing an accuracy within ±0.4 % strain. Hardness tests were conducted using a Vickers hardness tester under a load of 10 kgf. All tests were repeated five times for each condition to ensure statistical reliability. The volume fraction of RA and elongation are reported to one decimal place to reflect measurement precision and thereby facilitate the identification of statistically significant differences between samples.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
Fig. 2 
                       shows typical SEM and TEM micrographs of the initial cold-rolled pearlite microstructure before fast heating. It consists of alternately distributed ferrite (F) and cementite (Fe 3 C) lamellae aligned along the rolling direction, accompanied by a minor amount of grain boundary ferrite (marked by the red arrows in  Fig. 2 (a)). Chemical composition mappings of the cold-rolled pearlite obtained by TEM-based energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) reveal enrichment of Si and Ni and depletion of Mn and Cr in the F phase, with the reverse partitioning pattern observed in the Fe 3 C phase.

Fig. 3 
                       shows the SEM micrographs of CBT samples subjected to isothermal holding for various times. The reconstructed prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGB) based on misorientation angles, shown in  Fig. 3 (i), indicate a grain size of 19.6 ± 2.2 μm in the CBT-0 sample. For an isothermal time shorter than 10 min ( Fig. 3 (b) and (c)), a limited number of conventional bainite sheaves that formed along grain boundaries within the martensite matrix can be detected. With increasing isothermal time, the proportion of bainite sheaves markedly increases, accompanied by a gradual reduction in the size and fraction of martensite/austenite (M/A) islands, consistent with existing literature [ 25 , 26 ].

Fig. 4 
                       presents TEM results for CBT samples after various isothermal transformation times. The constituent phases for each condition were determined by integrating information from bright-field/dark-field images and analysis of selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns.  Fig. 4 (a) and (b) reveal newly formed martensite (position 1) transformed from unstable RA and a minor fraction of untransformed RA (position 2) after isothermal transformation for 15 min. When the isothermal time extends to 30 min ( Fig. 4 (c) and (d)), BF laths growing from grain boundaries into the interior (position 3), along with blocky martensite at the boundaries (position 4), can be observed. According to  Fig. 4 (e) and (f), further increasing the isothermal time to 60 min leads to the formation of blocky M/A islands (position 5), as identified from SAED. When the isothermal time reaches 90 min, blocky RA with a size of approximately 300 nm is retained (position 6). Meanwhile, the SAED pattern acquired from position 7 in  Fig. 4 (g) confirms that the BF and RA in the CBT-90 sample satisfy the Kurdjumov-Sachs (K–S) orientation relationship.  Fig. 4 (i) shows concentration profiles of alloy elements across BF and RA measured by EDS line scans in  Fig. 4 (g). Element distributions are homogeneous between the BF and RA phases, as quantified by the formula x i /(x Mn  + x Fe  + x Si  + x Cr  + x Ni ), where x i  represents the atomic fraction of element i. This type of bainitic structure which exhibits a uniform element distribution, is termed conventional bainite.

Fig. 5 
                       shows the SEM micrographs of FBT samples subjected to isothermal holding for various times. Misorientation analysis on the reconstructed PAGB ( Fig. 5 (i)) yields a mean grain size of 10.2 ± 1.8 μm for the FBT sample. This value is considerably lower than that of the CBT sample, confirming pronounced refinement. This pronounced austenite grain refinement originates from two main factors. Primarily, the increased superheating during fast heating effectively reduces the critical nucleus size for austenite [ 27 ]. Additionally, the release of deformation stored energy from the cold-rolled microstructure, along with the high density of deformed grain boundaries, provides abundant nucleation sites and a significant driving force for austenite nucleation [ 28 ]. In contrast to the uniform bainite sheaves in the CBT sample, the FBT sample exhibits a duplex morphology comprising conventional bainite sheaves and heterogeneous bainite sheaves that feature a pearlite-like structure. A detailed description will be provided in the following section. As illustrated in  Fig. 5 (b), when the isothermal time reaches 5 min, a fraction of heterogeneous bainite sheaves can be detected, indicating accelerated bainitic transformation by the FBT process. Meanwhile, with increasing isothermal time, the volume fractions of bainite sheaves gradually increase, accompanied by a reduction in M/A islands. No measurable change in M/A constituent dimensions is observed upon extending the isothermal time from 30 to 90 min, indicating that the bainitic transformation is substantially complete within approximately 30 min. Additionally, the BF laths in FBT samples are shorter than those in CBT samples, due to grain refinement induced by cold rolling and fast heating.

Fig. 6 
                       presents the TEM results for FBT samples subjected to isothermal transformation for various durations. After isothermal holding for 15 min, the pearlite-like structure with pronounced elemental partitioning, featuring alternating BF and RA, is evident, as depicted in  Fig. 6 (a) and (g). Line scanning reveals enrichment of Mn and Cr, alongside depletion of Si and Ni, in the RA. The inheritance of chemical heterogeneity from high-temperature austenite, previously transformed from cold-rolled pearlite with elemental partitioning, explains the substitutional element enrichment observed in RA [ 20 , 29 ]. This microstructure characterized by heterogeneously distributed elements is denoted as chemically heterogeneous bainite. Fast heating combined with short-term austenitization converts the ferrite and cementite in pearlite into Mn-/Cr-depleted and Mn-/Cr-enriched austenite, respectively, forming chemically heterogeneous bainite upon subsequent isothermal transformation. The short isothermal treatment also leads to the formation of larger martensite regions (position 2). From  Fig. 6 (b)–(e), it can be seen that the length and dimensions of the chemically heterogeneous bainite increase with prolonged isothermal time. In particular,  Fig. 6 (d) exhibits the coexistence of conventional and heterogeneous bainite within a prior austenite grain. Compared to conventional bainite, the heterogeneous bainite exhibits considerably finer and shorter BF laths alongside a larger size of filmy RA with a more uniform size distribution. SAED patterns confirm that the K–S orientation relationship is also satisfied between RA and BF in the heterogeneous bainite (positions 4 and 5). EDS results in  Fig. 6 (h) show significant compositional heterogeneity in the heterogeneous bainite of the FBT-90 sample, which is consistent with the elemental distribution observed in the FBT-15 sample, whereas the conventional bainite exhibits uniform elemental distribution similar to that in the CBT sample ( Fig. 6 (i)).

Following the morphological criteria established in Refs. [ 30 , 31 ], RA can be categorized into three types based on scale: blocky (0.7–2 μm), coarse filmy (0.1–0.7 μm) and fine filmy (<0.1 μm). Based on SEM and TEM observations ( Figs. 3–6 ), the distributions of filmy RA thickness and blocky RA equivalent diameter in FBT and CBT samples are summarized in  Fig. 7 
                      . Quantitative analysis indicates that the average size of blocky RA decreases from 2.5 ± 0.6 μm in the CBT sample to 1.4 ± 0.3 μm in the FBT sample. Conversely, the average thickness of filmy RA increases from 62 ± 16 nm in the CBT sample to 90 ± 20 nm in the FBT sample. Consequently, the CBT sample exhibits a higher content and larger size of blocky RA, along with relatively finer filmy RA. In contrast, the FBT sample contains more coarse filmy RA, which also displays notable compositional heterogeneity.

Fig. 8 
                       presents the XRD patterns of CBT and FBT samples subjected to isothermal transformation for various times, along with the corresponding calculated RA contents. With prolonged isothermal holding, the RA contents in both samples gradually increase. It is evident that the formation of more BF laths leads to increased carbon partitioning to RA during austempering, which increases RA stability and enables its retention at room temperature. Therefore, the RA content can be used as an indicator of the degree of bainitic transformation, with higher RA levels corresponding to a greater degree of transformation [ 25 ]. For isothermal times shorter than 30 min, the RA content is higher in the FBT than in the CBT sample under the same conditions. Notably, the FBT sample achieves an RA content of approximately 4.5 % after only 5 min, in contrast to the complete absence of RA in the CBT sample. This indicates that the enhanced bainitic transformation kinetics in the FBT sample results in a higher RA content under equivalent conditions. The accelerated transformation kinetics can be attributed to the collective mechanisms described below, as schematically illustrated in  Fig. 9 
                      . Firstly, cold rolling aligns the pearlite structure along the rolling direction. The dissolution of these deformed cementite lamellae during austenitization generates localized bands enriched with alloying elements, thereby creating adjacent regions that are depleted in these elements. These Mn-/Cr-depleted zones within the chemically heterogeneous austenite not only provide preferential sites for bainite nucleation but also guide the growth of bainite sheaves along the rolling direction. This preferential nucleation behavior stems from an enhanced thermodynamic driving force for phase transformation coupled with a reduced activation energy barrier, thereby accelerating subsequent lath growth [ 32–34 ]. Moreover, the reduced carbon activity caused by elevated Mn/Cr levels promotes carbon diffusion away from depleted areas to enriched ones, thereby enhancing ferrite transformation kinetics in the Mn-/Cr-depleted austenite regions [ 35 , 36 ]. Finally, cold rolling and fast austenitization result in austenite grain refinement, which provides more nucleation sites for bainite, thus improving its formation rate [ 37 , 38 ].

During the isothermal period from 30 to 90 min, the RA content in the FBT sample changes slowly and eventually stabilizes, which contrasts with the continual increase seen in the CBT sample. Meanwhile, upon reaching an isothermal time of 90 min, the CBT sample possesses a greater content of RA compared to the FBT sample.  Fig. 8 (c) also shows the change in hardness of the CBT and FBT samples as a function of isothermal time. When the isothermal time is less than 30 min, the hardness of CBT is consistently higher than that of FBT at the same time. Compared to the FBT sample, the shorter austempering time of the CBT sample resulted in less bainitic transformation. Consequently, a greater proportion of RA transformed into martensite upon cooling, resulting in higher hardness because BF lath is softer than martensite. After exceeding 30 min, the hardness of the FBT samples stabilizes at a minimum value of approximately 460 HV, whereas that of the CBT continues to decrease, reaching a minimum of 440 HV after 90 min. The differences in hardness also provide evidence of the distinct transformation kinetics.

The engineering stress-strain curves and corresponding comparisons of mechanical properties for various samples are presented in  Fig. 10 
                      (a)–(d) and  Table 1 
                      . As the isothermal time increases from 15 to 90 min, the yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of both the CBT and FBT samples progressively decrease, whereas the uniform elongation (UE) and total elongation (TE) exhibit an upward trend. Concurrently, for shorter isothermal times (<30 min), the CBT samples exhibit higher YS and UTS relative to the FBT sample, as their slower bainitic transformation results in a higher martensite content, which provides superior strengthening compared to BF. This mechanical constraint from the hard martensitic matrix on the RA elevates the critical stress for the TRIP effect, thereby accounting for the reduced elongation [ 39 ]. With prolonged holding time, the FBT samples exhibit higher tensile strength than the CBT samples. Nevertheless, across all identical isothermal treatments, the UE and TE values of the FBT samples are noticeably higher than those of the CBT samples. Specifically, the UE and TE values of the CBT samples after less than 30 min of isothermal transformation are nearly identical and lower than those of the FBT counterparts. This mechanical response is consistent with a brittle fracture behavior. As the isothermal time increases from 30 to 60 min, the elongation gaps between the CBT and FBT samples progressively narrow, which is attributed to notable bainitic transformation in the CBT samples over this duration. Meanwhile, for the FBT samples, increasing the isothermal time from 60 to 90 min results in negligible variations in both strength and elongation. This indicates that no apparent further bainitic transformation takes place, leading to equivalent mechanical performance. Conversely, the CBT samples exhibit a significant decrease in YS (from 940 to 880 MPa) alongside a slight increase in both UE (from 8.4 % to 8.8 %) and TE (from 11.0 % to 13.5 %). The increase in bainite content at the expense of fresh martensite accounts for the concomitant reduction in strength and enhancement in ductility.

Fig. 10 (e) shows the XRD patterns of various samples after tensile fracture, with the corresponding RA volume fraction and transformation ratio presented in  Fig. 10 (f). As the isothermal holding time increases, the RA transformation ratio in CBT samples first increases and then decreases, while in FBT samples it increases monotonically. This distinct trend is attributed to differences in the mechanical stability of the RA. After shorter isothermal times, the RA in CBT samples is predominantly blocky and exhibits low mechanical stability, facilitating its transformation to martensite during deformation. With extended holding, however, the fraction of highly stable filmy RA increases, suppressing the strain-induced transformation and reducing the transformation ratio [ 40 ]. In FBT samples, longer isothermal times promote the formation of coarse filmy RA with intermediate stability. This morphology acts as a transitional type between blocky and fine filmy RA, allowing continued transformation and thereby enhancing the RA transformation ratio progressively. At relatively short isothermal holding times (<30 min), the FBT samples possess a higher RA content at the fracture surfaces yet demonstrate a similar RA transformation ratio compared to that of the CBT samples. This observation can be linked to the higher initial RA content present in the FBT samples prior to deformation. With prolonged isothermal time, the RA content at the fracture surfaces of the CBT samples progressively increases, significantly exceeding that of the FBT samples.

To evaluate the deformation-induced response of RA, interrupted tensile tests were conducted on CBT-90 and FBT-90 samples. Tests were intermittently halted at prescribed engineering strains of 1 %, 3 %, 5 %, 7 %, at the onset of necking (9 % for CBT-90 and 10 % for FBT-90) and at fracture. The XRD patterns in  Fig. 11 
                      (a) and (b) show that the diffraction peaks of (200)γ, (220)γ and (311)γ progressively decrease with increasing strain. Meanwhile, pronounced austenite peaks remain in the CBT sample at fracture but are almost absent in the FBT sample. This suggests a nearly complete transformation of RA to martensite in the FBT sample, in contrast to the considerable amount of untransformed RA retained in the CBT sample. The change in RA content during the staged tensile tests, as derived from XRD patterns, is presented in  Fig. 11 (c) and (d). As strain increases, a continuous decline in RA volume fraction can be observed in both samples, offering direct evidence of deformation-induced martensitic transformation. However, the transformation kinetics of RA differ between the two samples. The CBT-90 sample exhibits a distinct two-stage reduction in RA volume fraction: an initial rapid decrease followed by a slow decline with increasing strain, with approximately 5.4 % RA retained at fracture. Conversely, beyond a strain of 5 %, the RA in the FBT-90 sample decreases approximately linearly with strain, reaching a final fraction of just 2.0 % at fracture.

The stress-strain curves presented in  Fig. 11 (c) and (d) show that the FBT-90 sample exhibits superior UTS and TE compared to the CBT-90 sample, indicating better overall mechanical performance. The RA in the CBT-90 sample features a combination of large blocky morphology along the grain boundaries and a fine filmy morphology embedded between the BF laths, as shown in  Fig. 3(h) and 12(a) 
                      . Conversely, the FBT-90 sample contains smaller blocky RA and an appreciable amount of coarse filmy RA adjacent to prior austenite grain boundaries, as illustrated in  Fig. 5(h) and 12(e) . Research has shown that blocky RA exhibits lower mechanical stability and is prone to deformation-induced martensitic transformation, while fine filmy RA exhibits high stability against transformation during deformation [ 30 , 40 ]. Comparatively, the coarse filmy RA in the FBT-90 sample, which is characterized by Mn/Cr enrichment, possesses mechanical stability intermediate between that of blocky and fine filmy RA. The progressive transformation of this coarse filmy RA, following that of the blocky RA, thereby contributes to the enhanced UTS and TE [ 41 ].

Fig. 11 (e) illustrates the evolution of RA transformation ratio with the applied strain. Below 5 % strain, the transformed RA fraction is more pronounced in CBT-90 than in FBT-90. Beyond this strain, the transformation ratio in FBT-90 exhibits a continuous increasing trend, while that in CBT-90 saturates. Under low applied strain, the coarse blocky RA, which possesses lower stability, undergoes preferential martensitic transformation. Consequently, the greater abundance of blocky RA in the CBT sample accounts for its higher transformation ratio in the initial deformation stage. With progressive strain accumulation, the extensive distribution of coarse filmy RA facilitates a persistent TRIP effect, resulting in a pronounced enhancement of the RA transformation ratio in the FBT sample. During the later deformation stages, the high carbon martensite derived from the transformation of blocky RA in the CBT sample promotes the nucleation and propagation of microcracks [ 42 ]. Concurrently, the fine filmy RA, characterized by high stability, makes a negligible contribution to the TRIP effect, thereby yielding only a marginal increase in the RA transformation [ 43 ]. In contrast, the sustained transformation of the extensive coarse filmy RA within the FBT sample facilitates an evidently higher transformation ratio than that observed in the CBT samples under identical strain conditions.

Fig. 12  presents EBSD images of CBT-90 and FBT-90 samples obtained from interrupted tensile tests at engineering strains of 0 %, 5 %, the onset of necking (9 % for CBT-90 and 10 % for FBT-90) and at fracture. The microstructural evolution during tensile deformation reveals a distinct stage-specific TRIP effect. After straining to 5 %, the CBT and FBT samples exhibit a clear contrast in RA distribution relative to the untested condition: the former primarily features small-sized blocky and fine filmy RA, while the latter is dominated by a mixture of coarse and fine filmy RA. This suggests that the transformation of this blocky RA primarily drives the initial deformation stage. As straining progresses to the onset of necking, the RA in the CBT sample is predominantly in a fine filmy morphology. Conversely, the FBT sample features intermittently distributed coarse filmy RA along lath boundaries, suggesting a transformation stage dominated by this coarse variant. At the fracture point, only a minimal amount of fine filmy RA remains in the CBT sample, with a content comparable to that in the necking region. This similarity suggests that the fine filmy RA undergoes no further transformation after necking begins. For the fractured FBT sample, however, almost no RA is detected within the resolution limits of EBSD, implying that the coarse filmy RA continues to transform during the necking-to-fracture stage. This progressive transformation is due to the enhanced mechanical stability of the RA from Mn/Cr enrichment. The improved stability, in contrast to the blocky RA, enables a portion of the RA to be retained until the late stages of tensile deformation, thereby effectively improving the post-uniform elongation via a sustained TRIP effect.

Fig. 13 
                       shows the TEM images and corresponding SAED patterns of tensile fracture surfaces in the CBT and FBT samples subjected to isothermal transformation for 90 min. Analysis reveals that in the FBT-90 sample, coarse filmy RA (approximately 200 nm in thickness) has transformed into martensite (positions 2 and 3), whereas finer variants (<100 nm) remained stable (positions 1 and 4). The CBT-90 sample exhibits a comparable trend, in which most filmy RA below 120 nm remains stable (positions 5–7), with only limited transformation observed in coarse filmy RA around 300 nm (position 8). These results indicate that the coarse filmy RA undergoes the TRIP effect during tensile deformation, thereby positively contributing to the enhanced elongation. Conversely, the presence of a considerable amount of untransformed fine filmy RA in the CBT sample indicates its minimal contribution to plastic deformation, due to its high stability.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
Two processing routes were employed to produce the ultrafine bainitic steels, namely conventional isothermal transformation and a hybrid route integrating cold-rolled pearlite fast heating with subsequent isothermal treatment. The phase transformation behavior, microstructure evolution and tensile properties were comparatively investigated using SEM, TEM, XRD, interrupted tensile tests and EBSD. The main results are as follows. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Compared to the uniform elemental distribution observed in conventional bainite, the FBT process introduced chemically heterogeneous bainite consisting of coarse filmy RA with noticeable compositional heterogeneity. This process also resulted in the refinement of austenite grains and blocky RA, accompanied by a reduction in the RA fraction. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The measured variations in RA fraction and hardness confirmed that the FBT process accelerated the bainitic transformation. This acceleration primarily stemmed from an increase in nucleation sites due to prior austenite grain refinement and the preferential initiation of bainite in Mn-/Cr-depleted austenite. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The FBT process yielded superior tensile properties compared to the CBT process after identical isothermal treatment. Under shorter isothermal durations, the FBT process effectively accelerated bainitic transformation, thereby increasing the RA content. This increased RA fraction improved strength and toughness via the TRIP effect. With prolonged isothermal time, the increase in Mn-/Cr-enriched coarse filmy RA with moderate stability, coupled with the refinement of blocky RA, contributed to sustained work hardening, ultimately enhancing the overall mechanical properties of the ultrafine bainitic steel. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            Interrupted tensile tests revealed distinct RA transformation behaviors under CBT and FBT processes. The CBT-90 sample exhibited an extremely high transformation ratio at strains below 5 %, dominated by blocky RA transformation. In contrast, the FBT sample showed a strain-dependent acceleration in transformation ratio, attributable to the prominent TRIP effect of its coarse filmy RA. Notably, the fine filmy RA in both samples demonstrated exceptional stability, remaining untransformed even after tensile fracture.

tables.caption: Summary of mechanical properties of the CBT and FBT samples subjected to isothermal transformation for 15, 30, 60 and 90 min.
